title: Eight

jokes.text: Artie catches Phil eating the shrimp and sends him away with 'Fat-free snackwells in the kitchenette.'
jokes.setup: Artie is furious that Phil is eating the guest shrimp again, clearly a recurring problem.
jokes.punchline: Rather than a real rebuke, Artie offers the pathetically inadequate consolation of Fat-free Snackwells — underlining both Phil's gluttony and Artie's withering contempt.
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie: the redirect to Snackwells is perfectly petty and character-specific. It's economical and sets up the show's tone immediately — nobody gets what they want, everyone is managed downward.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, damn it, Phil, how many times do I have to tell you, the shrimp are for guests?

jokes.text: Artie asks Brian to guard the shrimp as a legitimate security assignment.
jokes.setup: Artie is frantic backstage managing a major anniversary show with multiple celebrity guests.
jokes.punchline: His most urgent delegation is stationing a staff member to physically guard a shrimp tray — treating shrimp security as mission-critical.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist escalation of the shrimp bit — the joke is that Artie's priorities are completely inverted. Lands as a quick, dry laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Fat-free snackwells in the kitchenette. Get away from those shrimp, damn it, you bottomless pit.

jokes.text: Larry announces he won't perform during the kd lang segment. Artie: 'I don't. I never do.'
jokes.setup: Larry says 'Don't expect anything from me during the kd lang segment tonight' — framing it as a new, special warning.
jokes.punchline: Artie's reply reveals he has no expectations of Larry generally, not just during this segment — a brutal deadpan dismissal.
jokes.explanation: Economy is near-perfect — five words that reveal the entire Artie-Larry dynamic. The structure is airtight: Larry thinks he's flagging something new; Artie reveals it's his permanent baseline. Classic Larry Sanders character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Don't expect anything from me during the kd lang segment tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I don't. I never do.

jokes.text: Artie says 'let's make it quick' and Larry launches into a three-year story about squirrels dropping acorn hats into his jacuzzi.
jokes.setup: Artie braces for a quick story. Larry begins with 'kd rented the house behind me' and narrates a meticulous neighborhood grievance.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate complaint — squirrel acorn hats in the jacuzzi — is so petty and specific that it becomes absurd, and the climax (telling kd to go fuck herself over tree debris) is wildly disproportionate.
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-integrated — only Larry Sanders would nurture a three-year grudge over acorn caps and let it sabotage a career milestone. The specificity ('acorn hats,' 'jacuzzi') is what makes it land. Slightly wordy but the winding quality mirrors Larry's neurosis.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: She did nothing, so I told her to go fuck herself.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, so far, there's no surprise there.

jokes.text: Larry reveals he chopped off a limb of kd lang's tree and is going to carry that grudge onto the anniversary show stage.
jokes.setup: After establishing the neighbor feud, Artie asks about the show.
jokes.punchline: Larry confirms he intends to ruin his own anniversary show over a tree limb dispute — and his capitulation after Artie reframes it is equally pathetic: 'I'll just do my best.'
jokes.explanation: The joke is Larry's instant surrender once reframed — he had no real conviction, just neurotic resentment. Perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And that, by the way, is a milestone we never reached with any of our wives.

jokes.text: Artie: 'That is a milestone we never reached with any of our wives.' Larry: 'You speak for yourself.'
jokes.setup: The team celebrates the show's 8th anniversary.
jokes.punchline: Artie frames 8 years as an achievement no marriage of theirs survived; Larry's defensive counter-claim implies his marriage DID reach 8 years — the irony being both men are famously bad at relationships on this show.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical backstage joke about the sitcom's ongoing marriage failure theme. The exchange is fast and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You speak for yourself, Artie. I have some great clips from my last marriage.

jokes.text: 'What about the monkey grabbing your nuts? That's a classy one.'
jokes.setup: Larry has said they're doing a 'classy show with no clips.'
jokes.punchline: Hank nominates a clip of a monkey grabbing his genitals as 'classy' — entirely sincere, no self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Hank's complete sincerity — he genuinely believes this qualifies as classy television. The specificity ('monkey grabbing your nuts') is perfectly grotesque. Short, punchy, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What about the monkey grabbing your nuts? That's a classy one.

jokes.text: Larry only booked Mandy Patinkin so he can get good seats for the 'sondheim fuck fest at the Hollywood Bowl.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks if Larry booked Mandy Patinkin just for the show.
jokes.punchline: Larry confirms he booked a celebrated Emmy-winning guest purely as a transaction for Sondheim seats — and Artie's phrasing ('sondheim fuck fest') is perfectly contemptuous.
jokes.explanation: Artie's phrase 'sondheim fuck fest' is a great piece of comedy writing — contemptuous, specific, perfectly Artie. The joke exposes Larry's transactional relationship with his own show.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: So I'm to assume Mandy patinkin is only on tonight so you can get good seats for the next sondheim fuck fest at the Hollywood bowl?

jokes.text: Larry: 'I'm getting seats right behind home plate.' Artie: 'Get a foul tip.'
jokes.setup: Larry excitedly describes his Hollywood Bowl seating ambitions.
jokes.punchline: Artie wishes a foul tip injury on him — delivered completely flatly, not as a real wish but as a perfect puncturing of Larry's enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Three words that do everything. Artie's deadpan violent wishes for Larry are a recurring comedic register and this is a particularly crisp example.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm getting seats right behind home plate. Get a foul tip.

jokes.text: Artie: 'You're expecting a lull? Lull? Who said lull? I said Phil. Phil!'
jokes.setup: Artie says he'll send George Segal in 'whenever there's a lull' — then immediately panics at his own word choice.
jokes.punchline: Artie desperately backpedals, then summons Phil as if calling his name can undo the bad omen — superstitious producer magic.
jokes.explanation: Nicely absurdist — the idea that saying 'Phil' instead of 'lull' retroactively fixes the slip. Shows Artie's superstitious producer neurosis in a funny, compressed moment.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're expecting a lull?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Lull? Who said lull? I said Phil. Phil!

jokes.text: Artie asks Bruce to put hickeys on Larry's neck so he'll look like he 'had a good time last night.'
jokes.setup: Standard pre-show prep. Artie is managing Larry's appearance.
jokes.punchline: Artie requests fake hickeys as image management — implying Larry's real life is so sad he needs manufactured evidence of romance.
jokes.explanation: A bleak, funny detail that speaks volumes about Larry's romantic life and Artie's role as keeper of his image.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Lorenzo is the stupidest driver in history. He's supposed to pick up rosie o'Donnell. He picks up Chris o'Donnell and takes him to the rose bowl.

jokes.text: Lorenzo the driver picks up Chris O'Donnell instead of Rosie O'Donnell and takes him to the Rose Bowl.
jokes.setup: Rosie O'Donnell shows up having driven herself because the limo never arrived.
jokes.punchline: The driver confused 'Rosie O'Donnell' with 'Chris O'Donnell' and 'Rose Bowl' is close enough to 'Rosie' that it tracks as genuine stupidity — a great comic logic.
jokes.explanation: The setup-punchline structure is pristine — the confusion is internally logical (O'Donnell/O'Donnell, Rosie/Rose Bowl) which makes it better than random absurdism. This is a room-stopper. The image of Chris O'Donnell being bewilderedly driven to the Rose Bowl is delightful.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: I had to park 3 miles away, next to the day players from the Jeff foxworthy show.

jokes.text: Artie's escalating self-abasement to Rosie: 'I beg you on my late aunt's grave... I'll kill myself and all others like me.'
jokes.setup: Artie apologizes profusely to Rosie for the limo disaster. Rosie keeps saying 'I need more.'
jokes.punchline: Each apology is more extreme than the last, culminating in Artie offering to kill himself 'and all others like me' — at which point Rosie is satisfied.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is well-executed and the final line ('and all others like me') is genuinely surprising and dark. Rosie's 'Perfect' as acceptance is a great button. Shows Artie's bottomless capacity for showbiz groveling.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah? Well, you could try.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: Still more.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'll kill myself and all others like me. Perfect.

jokes.text: Rosie: 'I thought you were gonna have me change right here in the hallway.' Artie: 'I still love you.'
jokes.setup: Rosie is surprised to have a dressing room — suggesting she expected worse treatment.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I still love you' is pure showbiz non-sequitur affection — deflecting her complaint with charm. The joke is that this exchange IS the apology.
jokes.explanation: Functional showbiz charm comedy. Not especially original but pleasant.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: I thought you were gonna have me change right here in the hallway.

jokes.text: kd lang to Hank: 'Didn't recognize you without your chain saw.'
jokes.setup: Hank greets kd lang warmly backstage, presumably after their difficult history (implied by context).
jokes.punchline: kd fires back immediately with a chainsaw reference — implying Hank has done something violent or destructive to her (possibly related to the tree incident, possibly independent).
jokes.explanation: One of the best one-liners in the episode. The economy is exceptional — 'without your chain saw' does enormous work suggesting a full backstory of hostility. Whether it references Larry's tree chopping displaced onto Hank or an independent incident, it lands hard either way.

dialogue.speaker: kd lang
dialogue.line: Didn't recognize you without your chain saw.

jokes.text: Hank to kd lang: 'I can't wait, but then I've always enjoyed bleeding from my ears.'
jokes.setup: Hank says he can't wait for kd to sing tonight.
jokes.punchline: He then reveals he said this only because he 'enjoys bleeding from his ears' — a spectacularly insulting way to say he hates her music.
jokes.explanation: A classically structured insult — fake enthusiasm followed by devastating qualifier. The 'bleeding from my ears' image is both visceral and funny. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: kd lang
dialogue.line: I've always enjoyed bleeding from my ears.

jokes.text: kd lang: 'You still vacuum in the nude?' Hank: 'Why don't you get some blinds for that glass door, you sick fuck?'
jokes.setup: kd and Hank trade hostile pleasantries. kd asks about his vacuuming habits.
jokes.punchline: Hank's response confirms he does vacuum in the nude, that kd has witnessed this through his glass door, but frames HER as the 'sick fuck' for looking — complete inversion of accountability.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent comedy writing. The scene reveals Hank's nude vacuuming, kd's unwilling voyeurism, AND his total lack of self-awareness — all in two lines. The accusation 'you sick fuck' at the person who has SEEN you turns the power dynamic inside out. Highly character-integrated: only Hank could be both exhibitionist and morally outraged here.

dialogue.speaker: kd lang
dialogue.line: You still vacuum in the nude? Why don't you get some blinds for that glass door, you sick fuck?

jokes.text: kd: 'It kind of turns you on, though, doesn't it?' Hank: 'Oh, yeah. Mm-hmm. It makes me sick.'
jokes.setup: kd teases Hank that her seeing him vacuum nude actually turns him on.
jokes.punchline: Hank's response confirms it DOES turn him on before correcting himself — the 'oh yeah mm-hmm' slip is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Hank's momentary agreement before catching himself is a perfect acting beat. The joke depends entirely on Jeffrey Tambor's delivery but the writing sets it up cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It kind of turns you on, though, doesn't it?

jokes.text: Larry being sent to the bathroom before the show, and forgetting — then saying 'I already had juice.'
jokes.setup: Artie is sending Larry out for the show and asks if he went to the bathroom.
jokes.punchline: Larry forgot to go, then reveals he's already had juice — setting up the entire bladder crisis that will run through the episode.
jokes.explanation: The seed of the episode's best running gag. On rewatch, knowing where this goes, the 'I already had juice' line is funnier. Artie's 'Larry, you got to learn how to plan ahead' is a great, perfectly-delivered line.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: it seems longer than 8, doesn't it?

jokes.text: On the anniversary show, Larry says to Hank: 'It seems longer than 8, doesn't it?' and Hank responds with an extended awkward beat.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to do warm, celebratory anniversary banter with Hank in front of the audience.
jokes.punchline: The beat after 'it seems longer than 8' implies Hank agrees in a way that indicts their relationship — neither can fill the silence naturally, which is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders on-air discomfort. The live segment captures how stilted their on-air chemistry is, which mirrors their actual relationship. The show-within-a-show format makes the awkwardness meta.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Does it seem like 8 to you, Hank?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: Larry to Hank: 'I never get tired of you, and the sex is as fresh as ever.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to compliment Hank warmly on their 8-year partnership.
jokes.punchline: He uses the language of a romantic relationship — 'the sex is as fresh as ever' — applied to their professional partnership, then immediately gets flustered by his own joke.
jokes.explanation: An on-air Larry joke that reveals his genuine discomfort with sincerity — he turns the compliment into an off-color joke to escape real emotion. Then his own awkward justification makes it worse.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I never get tired of you, and the sex is as fresh as ever.

jokes.text: Larry: 'The reason is we have no expectations and it is always a surprise when it happens.' [extended laugh break]
jokes.setup: Larry is explaining why their partnership 'works' using sexual metaphor.
jokes.punchline: The 'explanation' — no expectations, always a surprise — describes the saddest possible sexual relationship, which he seems to find funny while the audience does too, but for different reasons.
jokes.explanation: Functional on-air Larry comedy. The joke works because it's revealing rather than clever.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I think the reason is is because we have no expectations and it is always a surprise when it happens.

jokes.text: Larry's Clinton joke: Clinton saw the million man march and said 'please, please take whatever you want. Just don't hurt my family.'
jokes.setup: Larry references the million man march in Washington.
jokes.punchline: Clinton's response frames him as a coward who misunderstands the march as a home invasion — plays on Clinton's reputation for conflict aversion and political triangulation.
jokes.explanation: Period-specific late night political joke. Competent but of its time — the Clinton cowardice premise is well-worn even for 1995. Functions as on-air monologue material.

jokes.text: Rosie O'Donnell blows off the pre-interview. Producer Paula says Larry 'isn't really comfortable with just winging it.' Rosie: 'What is wrong with him? It's a talk show.'
jokes.setup: Rosie insists she and Larry will 'just wing it' because they're friends.
jokes.punchline: Paula reveals Larry needs pre-written cards for everything, and Rosie's baffled reaction — 'how scared is he? You'd think the man could just talk' — is a perfect insider joke about how fake the spontaneity of talk shows is.
jokes.explanation: Great industry-insider joke. The irony that a talk show host can't talk without cards is the kind of specific showbiz satire this series excels at. Rosie's incredulity is the perfect audience surrogate reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Bill Clinton saw them out there and opened his door up and said 'please, please take whatever you want. Just don't hurt my family.'

jokes.text: Rosie O'Donnell does her own O.J. joke: 'He evidently believes the real killer is somewhere on the back 9.'
jokes.setup: O.J. Simpson has returned to playing golf after the verdict.
jokes.punchline: The 'back 9' framing — O.J. is literally searching for the killer on the golf course — is sharp dark comedy with good structural compression.
jokes.explanation: This is a well-constructed O.J. joke — the 'back 9' is a genuinely elegant image. High economy. Rosie's delivery and the backstage context give it cringe energy since she's pitching it as potential interview material.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: You know, what is wrong with him? I mean, how scared is he? It's a talk show. You'd think the man could just talk, all right?

jokes.text: Rosie: 'He got a triple-bogey on one of the holes, and tried to blame it on a Colombian drug lord.'
jokes.setup: Follow-up to the back-9 O.J. joke.
jokes.punchline: The Colombian drug lord excuse is O.J.'s alibi strategy translated into golf — escalating the previous joke's logic into fuller absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the prior joke. 'Colombian drug lord' is a funny extension of the O.J. defense strategy. Slightly less tight than the setup but the room reacts well.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: he's playing golf again. Evidently, he believes the real killer is somewhere on the back 9.

jokes.text: The ER sketch argument: Noah Wyle doesn't want to do the sketch, but as he and the writer argue about it, they ARE doing the sketch — and someone points it out.
jokes.setup: Noah Wyle refuses to do the sketch where he and Larry play ER vs. Chicago Hope doctors arguing over a patient.
jokes.punchline: As they debate whether the sketch would work — acting out the very dynamic of arguing doctors — someone points out they're already doing it.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best structural joke. The meta-comedy of performing the exact dynamic the sketch would require — competitive TV doctors sniping at each other — while arguing about whether that dynamic is funny is genuinely clever. 'Do you guys realize you're doing the sketch?' earns its 8+. It's original, well-structured, and the payoff is earned.

dialogue.line: He evidently got a triple-bogey on one of the holes, and tried to blame it on a Colombian drug lord.

jokes.text: Noah Wyle and Phil's ER vs. Chicago Hope argument: 'Your show is basically everybody's gorgeous and everybody's fucking everybody else.'
jokes.setup: Phil argues their Larry Sanders-style comedy is 'character-driven.' Noah argues ER is broader.
jokes.punchline: Phil's characterization of ER — 'everybody's gorgeous and everybody's fucking everybody else' — is both an insult and an accurate network TV critique.
jokes.explanation: Good industry-insider joke embedded in the argument. The meta-quality of Larry Sanders characters critiquing network TV is self-aware in a satisfying way.

dialogue.line: You're upset because nobody watches your show.

jokes.text: Noah Wyle: 'You're upset because nobody watches your show.'
jokes.setup: Phil is defending the artistic merit of their show over ER.
jokes.punchline: Noah Wyle cuts through all the artistic pretension with the one true Hollywood currency: ratings. The meta-irony is that Larry Sanders IS a critically beloved but low-rated HBO show.
jokes.explanation: Sharp meta-commentary. 'Nobody watches your show' cuts through the artistic posturing and is funnier because it's true of HBO at this scale. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Noah... noah, you're acting like a fucking 2-year-old.

jokes.text: An unknown man in the hallway is revealed to be a sportscaster — he has never been seen on the show and no one can figure out what sport he covers.
jokes.setup: Artie asks an unfamiliar man what he does. He says he's a sportscaster.
jokes.punchline: Nobody knows him, nobody knows what sport, he just exists in the backstage chaos. The joke is the pure randomness of TV infrastructure — people are always around for unclear reasons.
jokes.explanation: A minor absurdist detail — the TV set as populated by mystery people nobody knows. It's funny in a low-key way but underdeveloped.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah. I told you I should have peed before I went on.

jokes.text: 'Classy monologue.' Larry: 'Yeah. I told you I should have peed before I went on.'
jokes.setup: Coming off the anniversary monologue (which apparently went poorly).
jokes.punchline: Larry's takeaway from the monologue is his bladder situation — not the performance. The running bladder anxiety is escalating.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag beat. The throwaway 'classy monologue' from Artie (presumably ironic) followed by Larry's bladder fixation is a nice quick exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: I'm quick. I'll be sitting, but I'm quick on my ass.

jokes.text: Artie: 'It's my fault. I should have believed you.' [re: Larry's bladder]
jokes.setup: Larry claims credit for warning them he needed to pee.
jokes.punchline: Artie accepts full blame for not believing Larry's pre-show bladder warning — a completely absurd professional responsibility to take on.
jokes.explanation: Another good Artie self-flagellation beat. The idea that failing to take seriously a grown man's pre-show pee needs is a professional failure is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We had that when we had Chuck grodin on.

jokes.text: Rosie tells Larry she'll 'just wing it.' Larry privately panics. Artie: 'Paula? Did you see Rosie O'Donnell on Tom Snyder the other night?' Paula: 'I'll get the pre-interview.' Artie: 'Exactly.'
jokes.setup: Rosie has refused a pre-interview, saying she and Larry will just wing it.
jokes.punchline: Artie's roundabout way of ordering Paula to get the pre-interview anyway — referencing Rosie on Tom Snyder without explanation — implies Tom Snyder was a disaster that justifies why Rosie can't be trusted to wing it.
jokes.explanation: The economy of the Tom Snyder reference is elegant — we don't need to know what happened; the fact that Artie mentions it and Paula immediately knows to get the interview is a perfect industry shorthand joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We've been on 8 years.

dialogue.speaker: Mandy
dialogue.line: How long has Chicago hope been on?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We, uh, we're going in... this is our second year.

jokes.text: Larry asks Mandy Patinkin how long Chicago Hope has been on. Patinkin says they're in their second year. Larry: 'Wow. So you've been doing that show for a year and a half? Boy... 8 years we've been on.'
jokes.setup: Larry is interviewing Mandy Patinkin on the anniversary show.
jokes.punchline: Larry keeps redirecting the conversation back to his own show's anniversary — unable to stay focused on the guest. His 'Boy... 8 years we've been on' is pure self-absorption.
jokes.explanation: A perfect on-air cringe moment — Larry is ostensibly interviewing Patinkin but is really just using him as a prop for anniversary self-congratulation. Perfectly character-integrated: only Larry would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That is Mandy, uh, thinking.

jokes.text: Larry asks if Chicago Hope has ever won an Emmy, then immediately pivots: 'So are you doing a lot of Broadway now or...'
jokes.setup: Larry asks about Emmy wins — Patinkin's show hasn't won — and then doesn't wait for or process the answer.
jokes.punchline: The pivot away mid-question is the joke — Larry either didn't want the answer or lost the thread entirely. The awkward beat before the pivot is the comedy.
jokes.explanation: A great cringe beat — the non-follow-through after a potentially awkward question is pure Larry talk show incompetence portrayed with documentary intimacy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm going to ask you to tell me about your circumcision because I... Could tell from the way you're pushing this cd that you've had one.

jokes.text: Larry admits he doesn't have Patinkin's CD on set — it's on his desk — can't remember its name, but says 'I love the picture of you on the front. There's a picture of you like this.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants to promote Patinkin's new CD but clearly hasn't prepared.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't have the CD, can't name it, but compliments the cover design — the absolute minimum an interviewer can offer. His enthusiasm ('I love it. I'm not kidding.') makes it more painful.
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in the show's satire of talk show preparation — or the lack thereof. Larry's genuine enthusiasm for a CD he hasn't listened to and can't name is perfectly observed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've had 8. they keep going back for more, and frankly it is to the point now where it is whittled down to nothing.

jokes.text: Larry shows the CD cover — 'That is Mandy, uh, thinking.' [beat]
jokes.setup: Larry shows the Patinkin CD cover and tries to describe it.
jokes.punchline: 'That is Mandy, uh, thinking' — a completely useless description delivered with Larry's characteristic non-committal filler.
jokes.explanation: The 'uh, thinking' beat is a perfect small comedy moment — the inability to say anything useful about a guest's work while maintaining absolute confidence. Larry as talk show host at his most helpless.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: My brand-new $42,000 acura legend has a big Dent in it. Why, you might ask, do I have my own car here on the lot parked 3 miles away? Because the limo didn't show up! So farrah fawcett decided to hit my new car!

jokes.text: Patinkin: 'Open it up.' Larry: 'I will open it up. You're very pushy.' Then admits: 'We don't have a CD player here.'
jokes.setup: Larry is showing off the CD cover and Patinkin suggests opening it.
jokes.punchline: Larry calls the person whose CD he can't name and can't play 'very pushy' — then reveals they don't have a CD player on the set of a show that regularly features musicians.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Larry's unpreparedness to its logical extreme — they can't even play the CD — while he calls the guest 'pushy' for suggesting it, is a great comedy structure.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, Jesus, he's doing the potty dance. Get a clamp.

jokes.text: Patinkin asks Larry what he's going to ask him. Larry: 'I'm going to ask you to tell me about your circumcision.'
jokes.setup: Patinkin directly asks Larry what the next question will be — a reasonable request from a prepared guest.
jokes.punchline: Larry completely abandons the interview structure and asks about circumcision — an inexplicable pivot that's somehow the most confident thing he's said all segment.
jokes.explanation: The pivot to circumcision is funny in itself, but it's also setting up the episode's running circumcision thread. The timing and delivery make it a high-impact moment — Patinkin's confusion mirroring the audience's is perfect cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've never used the phrase 'inter-medical' before.

jokes.text: Patinkin: 'I've had 8. They keep going back for more, and frankly it is to the point now where it is whittled down to nothing.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Patinkin has been circumcised, presumably expecting a yes/no.
jokes.punchline: Patinkin claims to have been circumcised 8 times — a deliberately absurd number that mirrors the anniversary theme — with the horrifying image of the cumulative reduction.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's standout joke. The number 8 (mirroring the anniversary) is perfectly chosen. 'Whittled down to nothing' is an extraordinary phrase — visceral, horrifying, and funny. Patinkin commits to it with absolute seriousness. It's the kind of joke that references the calibration anchor ('Snip snap') — original, earned, perfectly structured, and genuinely shocking. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I suggest that you don't constantly look to the right.

jokes.text: Artie watching backstage: 'Tropical storm Larry's about to knock down a small wood-framed house. I've alerted the audience to head for higher ground.'
jokes.setup: Larry is visibly struggling on stage and there's a backstage crisis brewing.
jokes.punchline: Artie's meteorological metaphor for Larry's on-air distress — delivered with mock calm — is characteristic Artie fatalism.
jokes.explanation: Strong Artie line. The tropical storm metaphor captures exactly how he views Larry: a natural disaster to be managed, not a person to be helped. 'I've alerted the audience to head for higher ground' is a great extension of the metaphor.

dialogue.speaker: Fred
dialogue.line: Johnny wanted me to tell you how much he enjoys your show.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't you need to drain your lizard?

jokes.text: Rosie O'Donnell storms in furious: Farrah Fawcett hit her brand-new $42,000 Acura Legend — and Rosie had to park 3 miles away because the limo didn't show up.
jokes.setup: The limo disaster from earlier is compounding — now Rosie's car has been hit.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'no limo' to 'parked 3 miles away' to 'Farrah Fawcett dented my new car' is a perfect comedy of compounding disasters.
jokes.explanation: The running limo gag pays off with a new escalation — Farrah Fawcett is a funny specific choice. The comedy is in the accumulation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What else did Johnny have to say?

dialogue.speaker: Fred
dialogue.line: Uh, nothing about you.

jokes.text: Larry does the 'potty dance' backstage while counting down to air.
jokes.setup: Larry desperately needs the bathroom while the countdown to air continues.
jokes.punchline: The 'potty dance' — an adult man literally dancing to hold his bladder before going back on national television — is visual comedy inferred from Artie's 'Oh Jesus, he's doing the potty dance.'
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of a talk show host doing the potty dance before going on air is perfectly undignified. 'Get a clamp' as the practical solution is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Clear the hallways, 'cause my dick is going to be out, and it's going to be spraying.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Get a clamp.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing the potty dance.
jokes.punchline: Artie offers the most clinical, deadpan solution to Larry's urological crisis.
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect economy. The joke is Artie's complete refusal to see Larry as anything other than a production problem to be solved with tools. 'Get a clamp' applied to a human being's urethra is absurdly clinical and very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Fred
dialogue.line: Thanks very much, but you haven't seen my lungs.

jokes.text: Larry introduces Noah Wyle: 'I've never used the phrase inter-medical before.'
jokes.setup: Larry introduces Noah Wyle by noting there might be 'inter-medical competition' between ER and Chicago Hope guests.
jokes.punchline: Larry interrupts his own introduction to note, apparently sincerely, that he's never used 'inter-medical' before — which is both self-aware and completely derailing.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Larry Sanders on-air moment — he breaks his own introduction to footnote his own awkward word choice, which is both self-aware and more awkward. Only Larry would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Somebody's in here.

jokes.text: Noah Wyle: 'I don't watch your show either.' Patinkin: 'I knew we were going to get into it.'
jokes.setup: The mutual professional contempt between the two TV doctors is escalating on air.
jokes.punchline: The mutual declaration of not watching each other's shows — while being guests on the same talk show — is perfectly absurd. Patinkin's resigned 'I knew we were going to get into it' is the button.
jokes.explanation: The backstage argument has migrated to the on-air segment — the meta-comedy of this is satisfying. The callback makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Fred
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, but this takes a lot longer than it used to.

jokes.text: Larry to Patinkin: 'I suggest that you don't constantly look to the right.'
jokes.setup: Larry is moderating the increasingly hostile exchange between Wyle and Patinkin.
jokes.punchline: Rather than address the conflict, Larry issues a specific stage direction about eye contact — managing the visual optics rather than the actual problem.
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry — his instinct is to fix the camera presentation rather than the interpersonal problem. The specificity of 'to the right' is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Farrah
dialogue.line: I just nicked her car. You know, the morons at the gate are making such a big deal about this.

jokes.text: Artie tells George Segal to 'Suggest that you don't constantly look to the right.' Segal: 'OK.' Larry (on-air): 'I suggest that you don't constantly look to the right.'
jokes.setup: Artie coaches George Segal on camera behavior from the monitor
jokes.punchline: Larry relays the direction to Noah live on-air as if it's his own observation, exposing the completely managed nature of his spontaneous-seeming hosting
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of industry satire — the host is just a relay system for the producer's directions. Larry parroting Artie's notes live on-air as if they're his own instincts beautifully illustrates the artificial construction of TV spontaneity.

dialogue.speaker: Farrah Fawcett
dialogue.line: I just nicked her car. You know, the morons at the gate are making such a big deal about this.

jokes.text: Larry asks Wyle if he'll be naked with his on-air love interest. Then asks again. Then a third time. 'Maybe, maybe, yeah.'
jokes.setup: Larry is asking about Wyle's upcoming romantic storyline on ER.
jokes.punchline: Larry asks about nudity three times despite getting non-answers — his naked persistence about nakedness is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry talk show cringe — the repeated nudity question when the guest clearly won't give a satisfying answer. Character-integrated but not especially novel.

dialogue.speaker: George Segal
dialogue.line: I'm going.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. No, no, no. Just take it...

jokes.text: Artie greets Fred de Cordova (Johnny Carson's former Tonight Show producer): 'You great son of a bitch indeed. You look fucking terrific, buddy. And your vocabulary has really improved.' De Cordova: 'I've been watching the show.'
jokes.setup: Fred de Cordova visits the backstage to congratulate them on the anniversary.
jokes.punchline: Artie praises de Cordova's improved vocabulary; de Cordova reveals he learned to swear by watching The Larry Sanders Show — a meta-joke about HBO's content vs. network TV.
jokes.explanation: A nice insider joke — de Cordova is a real TV legend, and the joke about HBO's profanity corrupting the genteel Tonight Show producer is well-observed industry comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Did he get circumcised?

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: Yes, he did, in fact. I was listening.

jokes.text: Fred de Cordova mentions Johnny Carson. Artie: 'Don't you need to drain your lizard?' — to Larry, forcing him to move on despite the mention of his idol.
jokes.setup: Fred de Cordova mentions that Johnny Carson 'enjoys' the show — a massive compliment that stops Larry cold.
jokes.punchline: Artie short-circuits Larry's Carson fixation with the most unglamorous possible redirect: 'Don't you need to drain your lizard?' — prioritizing bladder management over idol worship.
jokes.explanation: This joke works on two levels: it calls back the bladder running gag AND exploits Larry's well-established Carson fixation. The juxtaposition of 'Johnny says he enjoys your show' with 'drain your lizard' is a great tonal collision. The timing makes this a particularly sharp Artie moment.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: It's that insertion around the side to loosen the... and the mother was crying, being... Look at all the men crunching over.

jokes.text: De Cordova: 'Thanks very much, but you haven't seen my lungs.'
jokes.setup: Larry compliments de Cordova on looking great.
jokes.punchline: De Cordova's deadpan reply implies serious lung disease — deflating the compliment with a specific organ disclaimer.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — the 'but you haven't seen my lungs' qualifier does enormous work. It's dark, specific, and perfectly timed. De Cordova delivering this with apparent sincerity makes it land. One of the episode's best single lines.

dialogue.speaker: Rosie
dialogue.line: Listen to me, Larry, a real man can hold his urine, OK?

jokes.text: Larry's bladder announcement: 'When kd lang is singing, I'm going to get up, I'm going to be coming back here to go to the bathroom. Clear the hallways, 'cause my dick is going to be out, and it's going to be spraying.'
jokes.setup: Larry briefs the crew on his bathroom plan for during kd lang's performance
jokes.punchline: 'My dick is going to be out, and it's going to be spraying' — Larry reducing his exit strategy to a graphic warning with total sincerity and no apparent embarrassment
jokes.explanation: An excellent peak in the running gag. The specificity and graphic nature of the warning ('going to be spraying') combined with Larry's complete matter-of-factness makes it a big laugh. The pre-planned escape during kd lang's set also pays off the grudge setup from the beginning of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This carpet can't take any more ur--

jokes.text: Larry: 'When kd lang is singing, I'm going to get up, and my dick is going to be out, and it's going to be spraying.' Staff: 'We'll form a runway all the way up to the bathroom.'
jokes.setup: Larry is desperate to use the bathroom and is planning his exit during kd's performance.
jokes.punchline: Larry's graphic description of his impending urological emergency, followed by the staff calmly agreeing to 'form a runway,' treats this as routine show logistics.
jokes.explanation: The running bladder gag reaches a peak of absurdity here — the staff professionally routing a spraying Larry to the bathroom is a great comedy image. The clinical planning around a bodily emergency is very Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This is the best anniversary show we've ever done.

jokes.text: Larry, mid-kd lang performance, rushes to the bathroom — finds Fred de Cordova already inside. De Cordova: 'Somebody's in here.' 'This takes a lot longer than it used to.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been holding his bladder through the entire kd lang song and rushes to the bathroom during applause.
jokes.punchline: Fred de Cordova — the elderly former TV legend — has beaten him to the bathroom and is taking longer than expected, citing his age. The bladder crisis meets a further obstacle.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully timed payoff — the bladder running gag collides with de Cordova's lung/age jokes. 'This takes a lot longer than it used to' perfectly connects both threads. The absurd dignity of de Cordova informing Larry from behind a bathroom door elevates the scene.

jokes.text: Farrah Fawcett confronts Rosie O'Donnell over the car incident. Farrah: 'I just nicked her car.' Ryan O'Neal shows up and is hostile to Larry because Larry bumped him from the show.
jokes.setup: The backstage chaos of the anniversary show includes the Farrah/Rosie car incident and an angry Ryan O'Neal.
jokes.punchline: Ryan O'Neal's non-sequitur arrival and grudge — he's mad about being bumped from the show — adds a new layer to the backstage disaster.
jokes.explanation: Functional celebrity chaos comedy — the backstage as a zoo of celebrity grievances. Ryan O'Neal's arrival is funny but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Farrah Fawcett to Larry: 'You sure smell good.' Larry: 'I've got to take a piss.'
jokes.setup: Farrah is flirting with Larry backstage during the show.
jokes.punchline: Larry's response to an attractive woman smelling him and complimenting him is to announce his immediate need to urinate — the bladder crisis obliterates all normal social function.
jokes.explanation: A perfect running gag moment — the bladder emergency destroying a flirtation with Farrah Fawcett is both funny on its own and a great callback payoff. The contrast between Farrah's romantic register and Larry's urgent biological one is pitch-perfect.

jokes.text: Ryan O'Neal: 'You're Irish, you've never been able to [kick my ass].'
jokes.setup: Larry warns Ryan that Rosie is Irish and will kick his ass over the car.
jokes.punchline: Ryan O'Neal turns it back on Larry, implying he's also Irish (Larry is not) or just generally escalating the backstage aggression.
jokes.explanation: A weaker backstage joke — the Irish threat gag is undercooked. More interesting as a chaos beat than a fully formed joke.

jokes.text: Pat O'Brien anecdote: 'I forgot my own name. We were doing the final 4...' — ends with producers feeding him 'you're Pat O'Brien' in his earpiece
jokes.setup: Pat O'Brien is sharing his story about forgetting Robert Parish's name and calling him 'big fella'
jokes.punchline: The story escalates to O'Brien forgetting his own name on live television, requiring producers to feed 'You're Pat O'Brien' through his earpiece
jokes.explanation: A well-structured anecdote. The escalation from 'forgot his name' to 'forgot my own name' is properly built, and the specific detail of producers whispering 'You're Pat O'Brien' through the earpiece is the perfect absurdist payoff. The story-within-the-show format works beautifully.

jokes.text: If there's a problem with my car, 'you can take me home, right?' Larry: 'I've got to take a piss.' — Farrah Fawcett asks for a ride home and Larry's entire response is his bladder.
jokes.setup: Farrah is suggesting Larry drive her home — a social invitation.
jokes.punchline: For the second time in this scene, Larry's response to Farrah's flirtation/request is simply that he needs to urinate.
jokes.explanation: The repetition amplifies the comedy — Larry now can't respond to ANYTHING that isn't bladder-related. The escalating single-mindedness is funny.

jokes.text: Pat O'Brien story: He forgot his own name on air. In his ear: 'You're Pat O'Brien. You're Pat O'Brien.' Larry: 'Did you say finally, I'm the big fella?'
jokes.setup: Pat O'Brien tells a story about being so exhausted from 18 halftime shows that he forgot his own name on air.
jokes.punchline: Larry's callback to the 'big fella' nickname from earlier in the story — suggesting O'Brien might have recovered with his own nickname — is a good joke button on a strong story.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured payoff to the Robert Parish story. Larry's joke button ('Did you say finally, I'm the big fella?') is sharp and shows him at his best as a talk show host — genuinely funny in the moment.

jokes.text: Rosie enters after all the other guests: 'I'm finally out here. Jeez. A little crowded over here. It was like forever. I thought I'd never get out.'
jokes.setup: Rosie O'Donnell comes out as the final guest on the anniversary show — after all the drama of her parking, the car dent, the Farrah confrontation.
jokes.punchline: Rosie's complaints about the crowded couch and the wait — delivered to the on-air audience who know nothing of the backstage chaos — is a layered joke for the viewer who's seen everything.
jokes.explanation: A decent on-air moment that lands on two levels — the literal crowded couch and the ironic payoff after all her backstage misadventures.

jokes.text: Larry: 'We saved the best for last.' Rosie: 'That is so sweet.' Then he immediately leaves the couch.
jokes.setup: Larry delivers a heartfelt 'we saved the best for last' compliment to Rosie.
jokes.punchline: He immediately begins trying to get up from the couch — presumably to go to the bathroom — which undercuts the entire compliment he just gave. Rosie tries to stop him.
jokes.explanation: The bladder running gag pays off beautifully here — Larry literally gets up during Rosie's first segment. The comedy of the long-built sincerity ('we saved the best for last') being immediately demolished by bladder urgency is an excellent structural payoff. High impact because the audience has been waiting for this to happen.

jokes.text: Larry asks Rosie if her adopted baby got circumcised. Rosie: 'Yes. He had a bris.' Larry: 'So you used the mohel.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Rosie are discussing her newly adopted baby boy.
jokes.punchline: Larry brings the circumcision thread — established with Patinkin — to Rosie's adoption story, treating it as a natural conversation topic rather than an intrusion.
jokes.explanation: The circumcision running thread continues and escalates here — Rosie's answer gives the bit a new direction. Rosie's 'I was listening' acknowledges the callback explicitly, which is a nice moment of audience awareness.

jokes.text: Larry to Rosie on-air: 'Is your baby... I know you adopted him and all, but did he get circumcised?' Rosie: 'Yes, he did, in fact. I was listening.' — callback to the Mandy circumcision bit
jokes.setup: Larry is interviewing Rosie about her new baby
jokes.punchline: 'Did he get circumcised?' — the circumcision topic from the Mandy segment reemerges; Rosie's 'I was listening' confirms the audience (and Rosie) has been tracking the motif
jokes.explanation: A well-deployed callback. The circumcision motif from the Mandy segment is now a running thread, and Rosie's 'I was listening' acknowledges it with perfect meta-awareness — she's been in the building the whole time. Good structural payoff.

jokes.text: Rosie describes the bris in graphic detail: 'it's that insertion around the side to loosen the... and the mother was crying...' as all the men on the couch visibly cringe.
jokes.setup: Rosie is describing what a bris actually involves.
jokes.punchline: The camera presumably catches all the men cringing and physically contracting — Rosie even notes it: 'Look at all the men crunching over.'
jokes.explanation: A well-observed physical comedy moment — 'look at all the men crunching over' is Rosie calling out the room's reaction, which makes it meta and satisfying. The interrupted graphic description is also very funny.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I have to go to the bathroom. I have to stop the tape.' Rosie: 'You're going to stop the show? I just got here.'
jokes.setup: Larry can no longer hold it and announces on air that they need to stop taping.
jokes.punchline: Rosie's perfectly reasonable protest — 'I just got here' — against Larry stopping the anniversary show to go to the bathroom is the payoff of the entire bladder arc.
jokes.explanation: This is the climax of the episode's best running gag. The structure is impeccable — everything has built to this moment, and Larry actually stopping his own anniversary show mid-Rosie-interview is both completely unexpected and completely inevitable. Rosie's reaction, the audience's confusion, and the cascading attempts to manage it are all great. High impact because the payoff is earned.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I used to have a trough under here, and someone has taken it.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to justify stopping the show to go to the bathroom.
jokes.punchline: He reveals he used to have a urinal trough under the desk — then someone removed it — as though this is a standard talk show amenity and its absence is the real problem.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke. The revelation that Larry USED TO have a trough under his desk — and is upset it was removed — is a genuinely original and deeply specific piece of absurdist character comedy. It implies a whole world of previous bladder management, a previous trough, and someone making the decision to remove it. The image is unforgettable. Near-perfect scores across the board.

jokes.text: Rosie: 'A real man can hold his urine, OK? That's all I have to say.'
jokes.setup: Larry is making excuses for his inability to wait.
jokes.punchline: Rosie's declaration that 'a real man can hold his urine' — delivered as if this is self-evident wisdom — is a perfect nonsense moral position delivered with complete authority.
jokes.explanation: A good Rosie line — delivered with the confidence of an axiom. 'That's all I have to say' as punctuation makes it funnier. High quotability.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Don't make me laugh. I'm going to wet my pants.'
jokes.setup: Larry is negotiating to stop the show.
jokes.punchline: Larry's warning that laughter will cause him to wet his pants on live television is both a genuine threat and a perfect escalation.
jokes.explanation: A good line in the escalation sequence — the threat of on-air pants-wetting raises the stakes appropriately.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I used to have a trough under here, and someone has taken it.'
jokes.setup: Larry is desperately trying to explain why he can't wait
jokes.punchline: He references a trough — implying he used to urinate from behind the desk during broadcasts — with complete sincerity, as if this is a reasonable lost amenity
jokes.explanation: The single best line in the episode. 'I used to have a trough under here, and someone has taken it.' is a jaw-dropping absurdist escalation delivered with total deadpan conviction. The image of a late-night host with a dedicated under-desk urination trough — that this was apparently once a standard feature which has simply been removed — is both hilarious and deeply specific to the show's world. The economy is perfect (16 words), character integration is maximum (only Larry Sanders could say this and have it land), and the originality is exceptional. This is a genuine 8+ joke — comparable to anchor examples.

jokes.text: Larry: 'This carpet can't take any more ur...'
jokes.setup: Larry is explaining why they must stop the tape.
jokes.punchline: He begins to say 'urine' — then catches himself — implying this has happened on the carpet before. The incomplete sentence is the joke: previous accidents are implied.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The incomplete sentence — 'this carpet can't take any more ur...' — implies a history of accidents on this specific carpet, which retroactively explains the trough and raises horrifying questions about previous shows. Maximum information from minimum words. The self-interruption is the comedic device.

jokes.text: A PA appears with a pair of pants: 'Somebody said you needed a pair of pants.'
jokes.setup: The on-air chaos is escalating as Larry insists he needs to stop the show.
jokes.punchline: A production assistant has already sourced emergency pants — suggesting that replacement pants are a routine show contingency, or that someone anticipated this outcome.
jokes.explanation: The appearance of emergency pants is a perfect escalation beat — the staff has clearly done this before (or prepared for it), which makes the carpet line funnier in retrospect.

jokes.text: 'This carpet can't take any more ur...' — Larry cuts himself off before finishing 'urine', implying he has wet himself or is about to
jokes.setup: The bathroom crisis reaches absolute climax
jokes.punchline: Larry's unfinished sentence about the carpet implies the worst has happened or is happening — the punchline is in what he doesn't say
jokes.explanation: The ultimate payoff of the episode's defining running gag. The structure is exceptional — after 27 minutes of building, the joke IS the sentence that doesn't finish. 'This carpet can't take any more ur...' is comedy through implication and economy: the word 'urine' is never spoken, the incomplete sentence IS the confession. Maximum structure score because the whole episode is the setup for this one broken sentence. Truly excellent television joke-craft.

jokes.text: Episode ends: Artie: 'What an embarrassment.' Larry: 'Good night, everybody. This is the best anniversary show we've ever done.'
jokes.setup: The anniversary show has descended into chaos — Larry stopped it to go to the bathroom, causing a full on-air meltdown.
jokes.punchline: Larry's sincere 'best anniversary show we've ever done' while Artie calls it 'an embarrassment' is the perfect ironic button on the episode. Larry's inability to assess his own disasters is the character's defining trait.
jokes.explanation: A great closing joke — the ironic contrast between Artie's assessment and Larry's is perfectly character-integrated. Larry's delusional self-satisfaction is the show's central joke and this is an excellent final expression of it. Earns its high score as a structural and character capstone.

tmdb_overview: Chaos reigns as the eighth anniversary show tapes and Larry tries repeatedly to sneak in a bathroom visit during a commercial break.
